comments.author: @WashRollTech
comments.text:
You need to look at total Danish exports, rather than focusing solely on a company like Novo.  Denmark boasts an unusually high concentration of global market leaders in sectors entirely distinct from the pharmaceutical industry. Should one sector face a downturn, others are ready to help sustain the economy:
Maritime transport and logistics. Service exports play a massive role in Denmark, driven by giants such as Maersk and DSV.
Green technology and industry. Companies like Vestas (wind turbines), Ørsted (offshore wind), Danfoss (energy efficiency), and Grundfos (pumps) are global heavyweights.
Food and ingredients. Beyond traditional agricultural products—represented by companies like Arla and Danish Crown—Denmark is a world leader in enzymes and food ingredients, notably through companies like Novonesis.
Consumer brands. Companies such as LEGO and Pandora generate billions in revenue abroad, independent of the pharmaceutical market.
"Invisible" exports (goods that never cross the border)
Many foreign analysts focus exclusively on physical goods shipped out of the country via trucks or vessels. However, a significant portion of Danish exports—often categorized as "merchanting" and "processing"—consists of goods developed by Danish companies but manufactured abroad (e.g., in the US or Asia) and sold directly from those locations. While these still count toward Danish exports and GDP, this model renders Denmark less vulnerable to localized bottlenecks or trade barriers.

How ironic. Humanity has progressed so far that today, thanks to the internet, even someone like you can reach millions of people and potentially make a living simply by sharing opinions. And you use that very progress to sit on an imaginary throne and pass judgment on 197 nations. I have no problem with analyzing the world's problems. What I find deeply disturbing is the arrogance of sorting entire nations into winners and losers, superior and inferior, as though millions of human lives could be reduced to five colors. And here's the real irony: *that very mindset is one of the root causes of the problems you're pretending to explain.*
Far too many political leaders think exactly the same way. They divide the world into good and bad, superior and inferior, winners and losers. And then we wonder why the world is full of conflict. The difference is that they hold political power, while you have a YouTube channel. But the underlying mentality is disturbingly similar. Before declaring which countries are doomed, perhaps you should spend more time studying history, philosophy, and above all, humility. *Because perhaps what's really "screwed" isn't those 197 countries, but the way you look at the world.* Ranking the world doesn't mean you understand it. comments.text:
Citing IMF reports doesn't make a ranking scientific when you cherry-pick one metric per country and ignore everything else.

​Putting Samoa in Green ("probably fine") purely because of low debt and foreign reserves—while ignoring that it imports half its calories, suffers from the world’s worst obesity/diabetes crisis, loses its workforce to emigration, and sits in a cyclone zone—is wild. 

Even wilder is putting Paraguay, Costa Rica, Chile, and Cyprus in the exact same tier as Switzerland, Norway, and Singapore, while ranking Germany, Japan, Austria, Finland, and the US below them in Yellow.

​And placing Tuvalu and Kiribati in Yellow ("in trouble, but with a believable way out") because of migration treaties isn't a "way out"—that’s literally abandoning the country as it sinks. 

Fun video, zero analytical consistency. 

In essence a vaste of time.
